name: Omar Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the presses at Halvorsen Pressings, out on Canal Road. We stamp steel brackets and door hinges for car makers, big coils of steel going in one end and parts coming out the other. I'm in at six, check the die, run the first-off part to the quality bench, then it's feeding, watching, clearing jams and stacking crates till two. Eighteen years I've done it. It's loud and my knees know it, but I like that you can hold what you made at the end of the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The noise wears you down, and the targets. They put a clock on the board now that turns red if you're behind. What I like is the lads, honestly. I eat lunch with Dev, he's the die setter, and we've been arguing about football at the same table since before my kids were born. And I'm a union member, I go to the branch meetings. Not a big talker, but I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Every year somebody comes in with a new gadget and a slide show, and the presses still need a person feeding them. I'd probably share some joke about it in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, but AI isn't what scares me anyway. The robots are. Two years ago they put a robot arm on line 4 to move parts between presses, and three operators got moved off. That had nothing to do with clever computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Clock in, do the shift, keep paying the mortgage, keep the three months we've got in the credit union where it is. Maybe I'd finally sort the boiler at home that's been making that noise since last winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like a storm went round the town instead of over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arm on line 4 scares you more than AI. What happened to the three operators who moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the robot arm on line 4 scares you more than AI. What happened to the three operators who moved?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, does anything at Halvorsen bother you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two went to other lines, one took the early pay-off and drives a delivery van now. He says he's fine but he looks ten years older. The union got them the transfers, that's the only reason it wasn't worse.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said it was hype and the presses still need a person feeding them. I'd probably make a joke about it in the union group chat.
S0.think: Honestly it would be a relief, but AI was never what scared me; the robots are. I keep thinking of the robot arm on line 4 that moved three operators off two years ago.
S0.do: Keeps working his shifts at Halvorsen and paying the mortgage. Leaves the three months of savings in the credit union and maybe finally gets the boiler fixed.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with the usual low grumble about speed-ups and targets.
S0.quote: Like a storm went round the town instead of over it.
S0.fieldNote: Omar separates thinking AI from robots very sharply: the robot arm on line 4 is his real reference point. Even in the calmest picture he talks about owners squeezing speed, so his politics are already in the frame. The fight he knows is one he feels able to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this comes in, not after. I'd say it at the branch meeting too. Change is fine if it's shared, but it never is unless you make them share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be our line next. Line 4 was the test. If AI makes the robots cheaper and easier to set up, Halvorsen won't think twice, and I'm the one with the certificate from 2006 and nothing since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal: no compulsory layoffs, retraining paid by the company, on company time. At home, Leila and I would stop the holiday money and put it in savings, maybe get to five months. I wouldn't go chasing courses on my own, I'm not good at that, I'd want it organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when the foreman calls you into the office and you don't know why yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't chase courses on your own. What if the union deal doesn't happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't chase courses on your own. What if the union deal doesn't happen?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I'd probably hang on till they push me. I know that's not clever, but I've seen men my age go off on some course, spend their savings, and come back to the same gate looking for work.

S1.say: We need the union at the table before any of this comes in, not after. Change is fine if it's shared, but it never is unless you make them share it.
S1.think: It'd be our line next, because line 4 was the test. I'm the one with a certificate from 2006 and nothing since, so Halvorsen wouldn't think twice.
S1.do: Pushes at union meetings for a deal with no compulsory layoffs and company-paid retraining. Cuts the holiday money with Leila and builds savings towards five months.
S1.feel: Anxious and tight in the chest, unsure what's coming and wanting someone else to organise the answer.
S1.quote: I've seen men my age go off on some course, spend their savings, and come back to the same gate looking for work.
S1.fieldNote: Omar wants change handled collectively and is openly unwilling to retrain on his own. His caution comes from watching others' courses fail, not from laziness. He worries more for the non-union agency workers than for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down by law, and I'd mean it. I'd be at the meetings, I'd sign whatever needs signing. I'd say it out loud: you can't put a whole town out of work in two years and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? It means I'm finished at Halvorsen, and probably everywhere like it. Two years is nothing. The mortgage has eleven years on it. Three months of savings is three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, we'd cut everything. Sami's football club, the car upgrade we talked about, the takeaway on Fridays. I'd be on the union's emergency committee, and if they walked out I'd walk out. Once it arrives, I'd be at the benefits office and asking Leila's brother if we can lean on him, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's going. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums that don't come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the warning time of two years let you do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would the warning time of two years let you do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Nour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Two years is one contract round at work. By the time the union's got a meeting with management, the robots are already in the crates in the loading bay. I'm not someone who reinvents himself in two years.

S2.say: This has to be stopped or slowed down by law, and I'll sign whatever needs signing. You can't put a whole town out of work in two years and call it progress.
S2.think: It means I'm finished at Halvorsen, and probably everywhere like it. The mortgage has eleven years on it and three months of savings is three months, so two years is nothing.
S2.do: Cuts Sami's football club, the car upgrade and Friday takeaways in the first month. Joins the union's emergency committee and any walkout, then turns to benefits and Leila's brother once it arrives.
S2.feel: Sick and overwhelmed, lying awake at three in the morning doing sums that don't work.
S2.quote: By the time the union's got a meeting with management, the robots are already in the crates in the loading bay.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Omar runs out of road: the union is his only plan, and two years is shorter than one bargaining round. He would hate asking his brother-in-law for help but names it anyway. The detail of Nour thinking he makes the doors himself was hard for him to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but louder and earlier. I'd be telling people this is the window, five years, use it to get laws in place. Tax the robots, protect the jobs, keep people paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I still think I'm out of work by the end of it. Five years just means I see it coming. But it might mean I'm not the only one shouting, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote on it, first time I'd ever vote on one issue only. I'd go to the branch every month and help with the campaign, leaflets, whatever. We'd try to get savings to six months and pay a bit extra off the mortgage. I still wouldn't start some computer course, but I'd ask the union about what training they'd fight for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with something to do with my hands. That's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you still wouldn't start a course. With five years, why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you still wouldn't start a course. With five years, why not?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leila say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because what would I train for? If robots can do hands-on work by then, a welding ticket is just a slower way to lose. I'd rather put the energy into the fight. You can call that stubborn, Leila does.

S3.say: This is the window, five years, so use it to get laws in place. Tax the robots, protect the jobs, keep people paid.
S3.think: I still think I'm out of work by the end of it, and five years just means I see it coming. But I might not be the only one shouting, and that matters.
S3.do: Votes on this one issue, attends the branch monthly and helps with campaign leaflets. Builds savings towards six months and overpays the mortgage, but asks the union about training rather than starting a course himself.
S3.feel: Scared, but steadier than in the fast picture because he has something to do.
S3.quote: If robots can do hands-on work by then, a welding ticket is just a slower way to lose.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change Omar's view of the outcome, only his ability to act collectively. His refusal to retrain has a logic: he can't see a job worth training for. His partner's challenge, that he hides behind the union, landed and he half accepted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse not to. Shorter weeks, the company pays into a fund for the people it replaces. That's what I'd post, if I posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is a different picture for me. I'd be fifty-three. Kids through school, mortgage nearly done. I'd still lose the job, I think, but it'd hurt less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as Halvorsen keeps me and keep at the union. We'd pay the mortgage down hard. Maybe in year five or six I'd talk to the union about what training actually leads somewhere, if they can show me someone who did it and it worked. Until then I'd keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Ten years is long enough to see the kids settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years means you'd be fifty-three. What does that age mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said ten years means you'd be fifty-three. What does that age mean to you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union need to win for you to feel all right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad was let go from the foundry at fifty-four and never worked properly again. So it's not a nice number. But at least I'd know it's coming, he didn't.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse not to. Shorter weeks, and the company pays into a fund for the people it replaces.
S4.think: Ten years is a different picture for me: I'd be fifty-three, the kids through school, the mortgage nearly done. I'd still lose the job, I think, but it'd hurt less.
S4.do: Keeps working at Halvorsen and stays active in the union while paying the mortgage down hard. Considers union-backed training around year five or six, but only if he sees it work for someone else first.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe, because there's time to see the kids settled.
S4.quote: My dad was let go from the foundry at fifty-four and never worked properly again. So it's not a nice number.
S4.fieldNote: His father's layoff at 54 sits behind everything Omar says about age and time. Ten years makes him calmer but still anxious, because the end point hasn't changed for him. What he wants is a written guarantee, which fits his trust in collective deals over personal plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two years. There's no time to fight and no time to save, and I'm not a man who reinvents himself. What would help is a law that says if you bring in robots that replace workers, you pay them a year's wage per five years served and fund real retraining, run by the union, not some website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. Halvorsen, the box plant and the bakery are most of the jobs round Canal Road. If they all go at once it's not my problem, it's everyone's, the pub, the shops, the school. People forget a factory feeds a whole street.

headlineQuote: People forget a factory feeds a whole street.
portrait: Omar Baker is 43 and has spent eighteen years on the stamping presses at Halvorsen Pressings, making brackets and door hinges for car makers. He's a quiet union member, never uses AI tools, and his real fear is robots, not clever software, ever since a robot arm took three jobs on line 4. He stays calm if AI fizzles out, grows anxious with steady change and panics at AGI in two years, when the union, his only plan, has no time to act. Ten years lets him breathe because the kids and mortgage would be nearly done, but he still won't retrain unless someone shows him it works.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there's no time to fight it through the union and no time to build savings beyond the three months he has.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies that bring in job-replacing robots pay a year's wage per five years served and fund real retraining run by the union.
